To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

centrifuging, pipetting and vortexing can significantly increase the level of free hemoglobin and phosphatidyl serine exposure, while the level of hemolysis is significantly increased by elevated pressures.
centrifugation, vortexing, and pipetting significantly affect the level of free hemoglobin in plasma, as well as the mean cell volume and mean corpuscular volume.
the mechanical stresses imposed during blood handling can influence the results of RBC damage measurements.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of laboratory procedures on the mechanical properties of RBCs.
the impact of blood sample preparation on the results obtained from mechanical blood damage markers.
the influence of standard laboratory procedures on the measures of erythrocyte mechanical damage.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
all the tested procedures caused a significant release of hemoglobin from the red blood cells.

the standard procedures of centrifuging and pipetting of blood can cause significant alterations to the mechanical properties of the red blood cell, and thus, the results obtained by using these techniques may not be representative for the original blood sample.

the centrifugation and pipetting of human whole blood can induce significant damage to erythrocytes, as measured by the increase of free hemoglobin in plasma, and the changes in RBC population, and that these effects should be considered in experimental protocols and taken into account in clinical laboratories.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
centrifuging, pipetting and high pressures can influence the results of erythrocyte mechanical properties, especially the MCV, MCH and free hemoglobin levels.
centrifuging, pipetting and vortexing of blood samples can cause significant damage to red blood cells and thus influence the results of blood damage measurements.
blood handling procedures can influence the results of erythrocyte mechanical damage metrics and that these should be taken into account for experimental protocols.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mechanical stress induced by laboratory procedures may be an important confounding factor that needs to be accounted for in studies of RBC mechanical properties.
it should be possible to minimize the impact of laboratory procedures on blood damage metrics by careful experimental design.
the effects of laboratory procedures should be taken into consideration in the design and interpretation of studies on blood damage and RSC properties.
